1.meaning: An emphatic oath-opener. Though it looks like the negative particle 'no/not', here at the start of the oath it does NOT negate; it intensifies and draws attention to the solemn vow that follows, functioning like 'Indeed, I swear...' Many scholars read it as redundant-for-emphasis (the so-called 'extra' lā that strengthens the oath), so the verse means 'Nay! I do swear...' rather than 'I do not swear.'

parts.en: no / nay (here an emphatic oath-opener, not a true negation)

1.grammar: A fixed, indeclinable particle — it has no case ending or tense to change. Despite its surface look as 'not', in this oath setting it carries no negating force; it heightens the seriousness of the coming oath ('Truly, I swear...'). The superscript alef (ۤ) on لَاۤ is a Quranic orthographic mark signaling a prolonged (madd) vowel in recitation.

2.meaning: 'I solemnly swear / I take an oath.' A first-person declaration of taking a binding oath by something sacred, here introducing what Allah swears by.

parts.en: I (first-person singular prefix: hamzated alef أُ)
swear / take an oath (Form IV present-tense stem)

2.grammar: Present/imperfect verb, first-person singular ('I'). The PERSON is marked by the prefix LETTER — the hamzated alef (أُ) — which identifies the first-person singular, as opposed to ya- (he), ta- (you/she), or na- (we). The ḍamma vowel (u) on that prefix is NOT itself the person marker: in the Form IV imperfect ALL persons carry this u- vowel (uqsimu, tuqsimu, yuqsimu, nuqsimu), so it is a feature of the Form IV conjugation, not of the 'I'. This is a Form IV (causative-intensive) verb. The final -u ending is the indicative ('plain statement') mood: it states a present, ongoing fact — 'I am swearing / I do swear.'
2.root: ق-س-م (q-s-m) — to swear an oath, to divide/apportion

3.meaning: 'by this' — the oath is sworn 'by this [place],' pointing to a specific, present thing (the city of Mecca named next).

parts.en: by (the particle of oath here: 'I swear BY...')

3.grammar: A prefixed preposition bi- ('by') attached to the demonstrative 'this.' Here bi- is the oath-particle ('I swear by...'). 'hādhā' is indeclinable (it does not change form for case); grammatically it sits in the genitive position after the preposition, and it points to a single, near, masculine thing — 'this very [city].'

4.meaning: 'the city' — specifically the sacred city of Mecca, the object Allah swears by.
4.grammar: A definite noun, 'the city.' The -i ending is the genitive case. It is genitive because the oath-preposition بِ governs the entire noun phrase that follows — including this appositive (badal) of هٰذَا — directly. (Note: هٰذَا itself is indeclinable and shows no genitive ending, so البلد's case does not come from 'copying' hādhā; both simply fall under the rule of the preposition.) The al- ('the') makes it specific: not any town, but THE city (Mecca).

1.meaning: 'and you' — a parenthetical address turning to the Prophet (peace be upon him): 'and you [O Prophet]...', introducing his special status in this city.
1.grammar: A connecting wa- ('and') joined to the standalone pronoun 'anta' ('you,' masculine singular). This is a detached subject pronoun beginning a circumstantial clause ('and you [being]...'). Its final -a is simply part of the fixed pronoun form (anta), not a case ending — standalone pronouns do not decline.

2.meaning: 'one who is free / lawfully settled (in it).' It describes the Prophet as being in a state of freedom or lawful dwelling in this city — i.e., this sacred city is made lawful (ḥalāl) for him, or he is free of restriction in it.

parts.en: free / lawful / unrestricted (one for whom a thing is permitted)
nominative + indefinite ending (-un, i.e. nominative with tanwīn)

2.grammar: A noun/descriptor, 'one who is free/lawful.' The -un ending is two things at once: the nominative case (it is the predicate, telling what 'you' ARE — 'you are free') plus tanwīn (the -n sound) marking it as indefinite ('a free one'). So 'wa-anta ḥillun' = 'and you are [in a state of being] free/lawfully settled.'
2.root: ح-ل-ل (ḥ-l-l) — to be lawful/permitted, to untie/loosen, to alight/dwell

3.meaning: 'by this' — the oath is sworn 'by this [place],' pointing to a specific, present thing (the city of Mecca named next).

parts.en: by (the particle of oath here: 'I swear BY...')

3.grammar: A prefixed preposition bi- ('by') attached to the demonstrative 'this.' Here bi- is the oath-particle ('I swear by...'). 'hādhā' is indeclinable (it does not change form for case); grammatically it sits in the genitive position after the preposition, and it points to a single, near, masculine thing — 'this very [city].'

4.meaning: 'the city' — specifically the sacred city of Mecca, the object Allah swears by.
4.grammar: A definite noun, 'the city.' The -i ending is the genitive case. It is genitive because the oath-preposition بِ governs the entire noun phrase that follows — including this appositive (badal) of هٰذَا — directly. (Note: هٰذَا itself is indeclinable and shows no genitive ending, so البلد's case does not come from 'copying' hādhā; both simply fall under the rule of the preposition.) The al- ('the') makes it specific: not any town, but THE city (Mecca).

1.meaning: 'and a begetter / a parent (father).' A continuation of the oath: 'and [by] a begetter,' referring to the one who fathers/gives rise to offspring — broadly a parent.

parts.en: and / and by (oath particle here, continuing the series of oaths)
begetter / father / parent (active participle: 'one who begets')
genitive + indefinite ending (-in, i.e. genitive with tanwīn)

1.grammar: An active participle, 'a begetter / one who fathers.' The leading wa- here resumes the oath ('and by...'). The -in ending is the genitive case (required after the oath-wāw, just like bi-) together with tanwīn (-n) marking it indefinite — 'by a begetter.' Being a participle, it carries the active sense 'the one who does the begetting.'
1.root: و-ل-د (w-l-d) — to give birth, to beget, offspring

2.meaning: 'and what / and that which.' Here 'mā' is a relative word, 'that which,' setting up 'and that which he begot' — i.e., the offspring. (It is the broad 'what/that-which,' not the question 'what?')
2.grammar: A connecting wa- ('and') plus 'mā.' In this context 'mā' is a relative pronoun, 'that which / whatever,' linking to the verb that follows ('what he begot'). It is indeclinable — a fixed form with no case ending. The shadda (doubling) on the wāw, wwa, is idghām: the tanwīn — specifically the nūn sound (-n of -in) ending the preceding word وَالِدٍ — assimilates into the following wāw, merging into it and producing the doubled wāw. It is the tanwīn's nūn that is absorbed, not merely a vowel; this is a recitation/pronunciation phenomenon and adds no extra meaning.

3.meaning: 'he begot / he fathered (offspring).' The act of bringing forth a child; paired with the parent above to mean 'the parent and what they begot (their child).'
3.grammar: A past-tense (completed-action) verb, 'he begot.' The bare stem with final -a is the default third-person masculine singular: 'he' did it, and the action is finished. Together with the preceding 'mā,' it reads 'that which he begot' — i.e., the child produced.
3.root: و-ل-د (w-l-d) — to give birth, to beget, offspring

1.meaning: An emphasis cluster meaning 'most certainly / indeed assuredly.' It combines an oath-affirming 'truly' (la-) with a particle (qad) that, before a past verb, stresses that the action has definitely and already happened. Together they leave no doubt: 'We have most surely...'

parts.en: truly / indeed (emphatic affirmation, often the 'answer' to an oath)
certainly / already (particle confirming a completed act)

1.grammar: Two indeclinable particles fused for emphasis. The la- is the emphatic 'lām' that introduces the response to the preceding oaths ('verily...'). 'qad' placed before a past-tense verb confirms and intensifies it ('has indeed/already happened'). Neither has a case or tense of its own; together they powerfully assert the statement that follows.

2.meaning: 'We created / We have created.' The divine act of bringing into existence, stated in the 'royal We' used of Allah's majesty.

parts.en: created / brought into being (past-tense verb stem)

2.grammar: A past-tense (completed-action) verb with the subject attached at the end: the suffix -nā means 'we.' So 'khalaqnā' = 'we created' — the act is finished and done. Of Allah this is the majestic 'We,' expressing greatness, not number. Following 'laqad,' it reads 'We have most certainly created.'
2.root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q) — to create, to bring into being, to shape/originate

3.meaning: 'the human being / humankind.' The whole of mankind viewed as a single kind — humanity as such.
3.grammar: A definite noun, 'the human being.' The -a ending is the accusative case, marking it as the direct object of the verb — the one acted upon: '[We created] the human being.' The al- ('the') here is generic, meaning humankind as a whole rather than one particular person.
3.root: ء-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — humankind, sociability, to be familiar/at ease (the human as a social, familiar being). Classical grammarians dispute the root: many (e.g., al-Farrāʾ, and as reported in Ibn Manẓūr's Lisān al-ʿArab) derive it instead from ن-س-ي (n-s-y, 'to forget'), which changes the assumed morphological pattern. Both derivations are well attested in the tradition.

4.meaning: A preposition meaning 'in', 'within', or 'inside'. It places something inside a state, place, or condition. Here it conveys being immersed in or surrounded by a condition (struggle/hardship).
4.grammar: This is an indeclinable preposition (it never changes form). It governs the noun after it, putting that noun in the genitive case. It has no tense or ending of its own to explain; its whole job is to link 'created humankind' to the state 'in hardship'.

5.meaning: Hardship, toil, distress, or strenuous struggle. It evokes the idea of life lived amid difficulty and exertion, fatigue, and labor that wears one down.
5.grammar: A singular masculine noun. The final '-in' is two things at once: the '-i' shows the genitive case (required because it follows the preposition fī, 'in'), and the extra '-n' sound (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'in (a state of) hardship', leaving it open-ended and unspecified, which heightens the sense of constant struggle.
5.root: ك-ب-د (k-b-d) — to be hard/burdensome; strain, toil

1.meaning: 'Does he think / suppose / reckon?' A questioning of someone's mistaken assumption. The rhetorical question rebukes the false belief that follows, implying 'how could he possibly imagine...'.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb carrying a question. The opening 'a-' is the interrogative particle ('does...?'). The 'ya-' prefix marks a third-person masculine singular subject ('he'). The final '-u' ending shows the verb is in its plain indicative form (a simple statement of fact: 'he thinks'), now turned into a question by the prefix.
1.root: ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b) — to reckon, count, suppose, calculate

2.meaning: A particle meaning 'that', used to introduce a following verbal clause (like 'that he should...'). It turns the verb after it into the content of thinking, wanting, or supposing.
2.grammar: An indeclinable particle with no ending of its own. Normally it puts the following verb into the subjunctive ('that he do...'), but here it is followed by lan, which itself governs the verb. It links 'Does he think...' to the clause that follows: 'that no one has power over him'.

3.meaning: An emphatic negation for the future: 'will never' / 'shall not at all'. It denies that something will ever happen, more forcefully than a simple 'not'.
3.grammar: A negating particle that points to the future. It has no ending of its own, but it forces the verb after it into the subjunctive mood, which is why the next word ends in '-a' rather than '-u'. The doubled 'l' (shown as lla-) is just the recitation linking it smoothly to the previous word.

4.meaning: 'To have power over', 'to be able to', 'to prevail against', or 'to determine/decree'. Here it means to have control or capability over someone — the power to call to account.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb, third-person masculine singular ('he/one'). The 'ya-' prefix marks the 'he' subject. Crucially the final ending is '-a' (not '-u'): this is the subjunctive, caused by the preceding particle lan. So it reads 'that no one will (ever) have power'. The doubled 'y' (yya-) is recitation linking it to lan before it.

5.meaning: 'Over him', 'against him', or 'upon him'. The preposition ʿalā ('over/upon/against') joined to the pronoun 'him', expressing authority or power directed at that person.
5.grammar: A preposition with an attached pronoun. The base preposition ʿalā shifts to the form ʿalay- when a pronoun is attached. The ending '-hi' means 'him/it'. (The vowel is 'hi' rather than 'hu' here because it follows the 'ay' sound, a regular pronunciation rule.) Together: 'over him' — i.e., have power over him.

6.meaning: 'Anyone', 'a single one', or 'someone'. In a negative sentence like this it means 'no one at all' — not even one person.
6.grammar: A singular noun acting as the subject (the one doing the verb 'have power'). The final '-un' is two things together: the '-u' marks the nominative case (the doer of the action), and the extra '-n' sound (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'any(one)'. With the negation lan, it means 'no one whatsoever has power over him'.
6.root: ا-ح-د (ʾ-ḥ-d) — oneness, a single one (related to wāḥid, 'one')

1.meaning: 'He says' or 'he will say'. A verb of speaking; in context it reports a person's boastful claim. The present form can carry a future sense ('he will say') or describe ongoing/habitual speech.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb, third-person masculine singular ('he'). The 'ya-' prefix marks the 'he' subject. The final '-u' ending shows the plain indicative form — a straightforward report ('he says'), with no particle altering its mood. The long 'ū' is the hollow root's middle letter (w) surfacing as a long vowel.

2.meaning: 'I have destroyed / consumed / used up'. Here it means to have squandered or burned through (wealth) — to make it perish through extravagant spending.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb. The form ahlaka means 'to cause to perish / destroy' (a causative shape of the root). The attached ending '-tu' means 'I' did the action: 'I destroyed / I squandered'. Being past tense, it states the deed as already completed — a boast about wealth already gone.
2.root: ه-ل-ك (h-l-k) — to perish, be destroyed; (causative) to make perish

3.meaning: 'Wealth', 'property', 'money', or 'possessions'. It refers to material goods and riches that a person owns.
3.grammar: A singular masculine noun functioning as the object of the verb (the thing that was 'squandered'). The final '-an' is two things together: the '-a' marks the accusative case (the receiver of the action), and the extra '-n' sound (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'wealth / some wealth'. So: 'I have squandered wealth'.
3.root: م-و-ل (m-w-l) — wealth, property, to be wealthy

4.meaning: 'Heaps', 'masses', 'piles' — and by extension 'piled-up / abundant (wealth)'. It pictures wealth amassed in great compacted heaps, gathered together in vast quantity.
4.grammar: A noun in the accusative case, not an adjective. Classically lubad is the broken (irregular) plural of lubda — a matted, compacted mass or layer — so it literally means 'heaps/masses'. The '-a' marks the accusative and the extra '-n' (tanwīn) marks it indefinite. It does not agree with māl as a describing adjective would; rather it stands in the accusative as a ḥāl (a circumstantial qualifier: 'I squandered wealth, [it being] heaps') — i.e., describing the state of the wealth. The doubled 'l' (llu-) is recitation linking it to the word before.

1.meaning: 'Does he think / suppose / reckon?' A questioning of someone's mistaken assumption. The rhetorical question rebukes the false belief that follows, implying 'how could he possibly imagine...'.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb carrying a question. The opening 'a-' is the interrogative particle ('does...?'). The 'ya-' prefix marks a third-person masculine singular subject ('he'). The final '-u' ending shows the verb is in its plain indicative form (a simple statement of fact: 'he thinks'), now turned into a question by the prefix.
1.root: ح-س-ب (ḥ-s-b) — to reckon, count, suppose, calculate

2.meaning: A particle meaning 'that', used to introduce a following verbal clause (like 'that he should...'). It turns the verb after it into the content of thinking, wanting, or supposing.
2.grammar: An indeclinable particle with no ending of its own. Normally it puts the following verb into the subjunctive ('that he do...'), but here it is followed by lan, which itself governs the verb. It links 'Does he think...' to the clause that follows: 'that no one has power over him'.

3.meaning: A negating particle meaning 'not' that does a special job: it turns a present-tense verb into a firm denial of something in the PAST ('did not / has not'). So 'lam yara' = 'he did not see'. It always forces the verb after it into a clipped, vowel-dropping form (the jussive).
3.grammar: A particle of negation plus past-time. It governs the verb that follows it, putting that verb into the 'jussive' mood — the trimmed form whose ending is cut off (often ending in a silent/sukun consonant rather than a vowel). Although the verb it precedes is present-tense in shape, 'lam' shifts its meaning to the past: 'has not / did not'. (The doubled 'll-' here is just the running-together of the preceding word in recitation.)

4.meaning: '(that) he sees him' or '(that) anyone sees him' — the act of seeing/observing, with 'him' as the one seen. In context, paired with the preceding 'lam', the sense becomes 'that no one has seen him / observed him'.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('he sees'), with an attached object pronoun '-hu' ('him'). It stands in the jussive mood because of the earlier 'lam'; for this weak-final verb the jussive drops the final root-letter, leaving 'yara'. The 'ya-' prefix marks 'he'; the '-hu' suffix marks the object 'him'. (The long final vowel and hamza in the printed form reflect recitation lengthening at a pause.)

5.meaning: 'Anyone', 'a single one', or 'someone'. In a negative sentence like this it means 'no one at all' — not even one person.
5.grammar: A singular noun acting as the subject (the one doing the verb 'have power'). The final '-un' is two things together: the '-u' marks the nominative case (the doer of the action), and the extra '-n' sound (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'any(one)'. With the negation lan, it means 'no one whatsoever has power over him'.
5.root: ا-ح-د (ʾ-ḥ-d) — oneness, a single one (related to wāḥid, 'one')

1.meaning: 'Have …not…?' — a combination of the question-word 'a-' ('do/did/have…?') with the negator 'lam' ('not, in the past'). Together they form a rhetorical question expecting the answer 'yes': 'Have We not…?' It gently presses the listener to acknowledge an obvious truth.
1.grammar: Two particles fused: the interrogative prefix 'a-' (turning the sentence into a question) and 'lam' (negation + past time, which puts the following verb into the cut-off jussive form). The combination 'a-lam' is a rhetorical question — literally 'Have…not…?' — used to affirm rather than to ask, prompting the hearer to agree.

2.meaning: 'we make / we appoint / we give' — to make something into something, to assign or grant it. Here, with the preceding 'a-lam', it means 'Did We not make / give…?'
2.grammar: A present-tense verb, 1st-person plural ('we make'), shown by the 'na-' prefix meaning 'we'. Because of the earlier 'lam', it is in the jussive mood: its final letter takes a silent sukun (najʿal, with no case-vowel), the trimmed form 'lam' requires. The plural 'we' here is the royal/majestic 'We' of Allah.

3.meaning: 'for him / to him' — marks possession or benefit: that something is given to him or belongs to him. In context: 'Did We not make FOR HIM two eyes…?'
3.grammar: A preposition 'li-' ('for/to') with the attached pronoun '-hu' ('him'). When 'li-' takes a pronoun it appears as 'la-', giving 'lahu' = 'for him / to him'. The pronoun is in the object/genitive form required after a preposition. (The doubled 'll-' in the printed form is the running-together with the preceding word in recitation.)

4.meaning: 'two eyes' — the pair of eyes, named as one of Allah's gifts to the human being.
4.grammar: A dual noun — 'two eyes' — built from 'ʿayn' ('eye') plus the dual ending '-ayni'. The '-ayni' form (rather than '-āni') shows the accusative/genitive case: here accusative, because the noun is the object of 'najʿal' ('We made [two eyes]'). The dual ending itself signals exactly two, not a vague plural.

1.meaning: 'and a tongue' — the organ of speech, listed as a further gift. The 'a/an' sense (indefinite, 'a tongue') is carried by its ending.
1.grammar: The connector 'wa-' ('and') joins this to the previous gifts. 'lisān' ('tongue') carries the ending '-an' (tanwīn fatḥ): the double-'a' marks it as both indefinite ('a tongue') and accusative — i.e. the object of the earlier verb 'najʿal' ('We gave… a tongue'). The trailing alif is the spelling partner of this '-an' ending.

2.meaning: 'and two lips' — the pair of lips, completing the gifts of the mouth.
2.grammar: The connector 'wa-' ('and') links it to the list. 'shafa' ('lip') takes the dual ending '-ayni' = 'two lips'. The '-ayni' (not '-āni') shows accusative/genitive case — here accusative, since it too is an object of 'najʿal' ('We made… two lips'). The dual ending marks exactly two.

1.meaning: 'and We guided him / and We showed him the way' — to guide, to direct someone along a path. Pairs the act of guiding with 'him' as the one guided.

parts.en: guide / show the way (past-tense verb stem)

1.grammar: The connector 'wa-' ('and') joins this clause. The verb is past-tense ('we guided'); '-nā' is the attached subject ending meaning 'we' (the majestic 'We' of Allah), and '-hu' is the object pronoun 'him'. The original final root-letter of the verb appears as the long 'ā' (hadaynā-) before the pronoun. So the whole reads 'and We guided him'.

2.meaning: 'the two highroads / the two ways' — literally two raised, prominent paths; understood as the two clear moral roads, of good and of evil, between which the human is shown the choice.
2.grammar: The definite article 'al-' ('the') is attached; its 'l' assimilates into the following 'n' (so it is pronounced 'an-najd…'). 'najd' means a high, raised road; the dual ending '-ayni' makes it 'the two highroads'. The '-ayni' form marks accusative case — it is the object of 'hadaynāhu' ('We showed him the two ways') — and signals exactly two.
2.root: ن-ج-د (n-j-d) — high/elevated ground, a raised road

1.meaning: 'but/yet … not' — the connector 'fa-' ('so/but/then') joined to the negator 'lā' ('not'). Here 'fa-lā iqtaḥama' expresses regret over a deed NOT done: 'yet he did not undertake / would that he had undertaken…'. The 'lā' negates the past verb that follows.
1.grammar: Two particles: 'fa-' is a connector ('so/yet/then') linking back to the previous verses, and 'lā' is the negative 'not'. When 'lā' precedes a past-tense verb as it does here, it negates that past act ('he did not…'), and in this verse it carries a tone of reproach/regret — that the person failed to take the hard, upward path.

2.meaning: 'he charged into / tackled / braved (a steep, difficult thing)' — to plunge boldly into something hard and daunting, to take on a strenuous undertaking. With the preceding 'fa-lā' it means 'yet he did not take on [the steep path].'

parts.en: (form-VIII pattern: the i- beginning and infixed -t- of the 'eftaʿala' stem)
plunge in / brave a hardship (root in the verb stem)

2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('he…'), built on the reflexive/intensive 'Form VIII' pattern (iftaʿala) — seen in the helping 'i-' at the start and the inserted '-t-' — which gives the sense of plunging into something oneself with effort. The final '-a' (fatḥa) is the normal past-tense ending for 'he did'. So: 'he braved / charged into [the steep path].'
2.root: ق-ح-م (q-ḥ-m) — to plunge/rush headlong into something hazardous or difficult

3.meaning: The steep mountain pass or uphill road; here it is a powerful metaphor for the morally difficult, demanding ascent of self-sacrificing good deeds — the hard climb that the disbeliever has not even tried to undertake.
3.grammar: A definite feminine singular noun. The final '-a' (accusative) marks it as the direct object of an understood verb 'to attempt/scale' (he did not attempt the steep path). The closing tā' marbūṭa carries this '-a' vowel, showing it is the thing acted upon, not the doer.
3.root: ع-ق-ب (ʿ-q-b) — to follow/come after; a steep, hard ascent or obstacle (related to 'heel' and 'consequence')

1.meaning: 'And what…' — an opening that combines the connector 'and' with an interrogative 'what', here used not for ordinary information but to magnify and dramatize: 'And what could possibly make you grasp…'. It builds awe before something weighty.
1.grammar: Two indeclinable particles, so there is no case ending to change. 'Wa-' simply joins this to what precedes; 'mā' is an interrogative 'what' functioning as the subject of the rhetorical question. The long final vowel (mā) is fixed and never inflects. (The lengthening mark before the next word is for recitation.)

2.meaning: 'Has made you know / can make you realize' — to cause someone to attain knowledge of something. The form implies that only a higher disclosure could convey the true magnitude of the matter; human reckoning alone cannot.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('it/he made known'), in the causative pattern (afʿala) — 'to make someone perceive'. The attached '-ka' is the object pronoun 'you' (addressing the Prophet). There is no separate subject suffix; the bare verb already means 'he/it'. So the whole means 'what has made you know'.
2.root: د-ر-ي (d-r-y) — to know, to perceive, to be aware

3.meaning: 'What' — the interrogative 'what', here introducing the indirect question whose answer the next verses give: '…what the steep path is.' It points forward to the explanation that follows.
3.grammar: An indeclinable interrogative particle with no case ending; its form never changes. Here it acts as the subject ('what?') of the clause that the following noun completes, setting up the question 'what is the steep path?'.

4.meaning: The steep mountain pass / the demanding uphill road — the same metaphor for the arduous course of righteous, self-sacrificing deeds, now named as the subject being asked about: 'what is the steep path?'
4.grammar: A definite feminine singular noun. The final '-u' (nominative) marks it as the subject of the rhetorical question ('what IS the steep path?'). Contrast id 36, where the same word ended in '-a' as an object; here the '-u' shows it is the thing being talked about, not acted upon.
4.root: ع-ق-ب (ʿ-q-b) — to follow/come after; a steep, hard ascent or obstacle

1.meaning: The act of freeing, releasing, or untying — here specifically the loosing of a bound human being, i.e. emancipating a slave. It conveys breaking a yoke and restoring someone's freedom.
1.grammar: A verbal noun (the name of the action 'freeing'), masculine singular. The final '-u' (nominative) marks it as the subject/predicate of the sentence — 'It is (the) freeing…'. The doubled 'k' (shadda) is part of the root, not a separate piece. It stands in a possessive link to the next word ('freeing OF a neck').
1.root: ف-ك-ك (f-k-k) — to separate, unfasten, set loose, disjoin

2.meaning: Literally 'a neck' — but idiomatically a whole human person, and especially a bondsman or slave. 'Freeing a neck' is the Qur'anic expression for emancipating an enslaved human being.
2.grammar: An indefinite feminine singular noun. The '-in' ending is genitive with nunation ('-n'): genitive because it is possessed by the preceding verbal noun ('freeing OF a neck'), and the '-n' (tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'a neck', any enslaved person.
2.root: ر-ق-ب (r-q-b) — neck; to watch over, guard, keep under observation

1.meaning: 'Or' — a particle offering an alternative, here presenting a second equally praiseworthy deed beside freeing a slave: emancipation OR feeding the hungry.
1.grammar: An indeclinable conjunction with no case ending. It links two alternatives, joining the act of 'feeding' that follows to the act of 'freeing' that came before, presenting them as parallel options.

2.meaning: The act of feeding — giving food to others. As a verbal noun it names the deed itself: providing nourishment, especially to those gripped by hunger.

parts.en: prefixed vowel of the verbal-noun pattern (ifʿāl)

2.grammar: A verbal noun of the causative (afʿala) pattern, masculine singular, meaning 'the giving of food'. The '-un' ending is nominative with nunation ('-n'): nominative because it is parallel to 'freeing' (fakku) as a predicate ('or [it is] feeding…'), and the '-n' marks it as indefinite. It is followed by the prepositional phrase 'fī yawmin' ('on a day…') that specifies when.
2.root: ط-ع-م (ṭ-ʿ-m) — food, to feed, to taste/eat

3.meaning: A preposition meaning 'in', 'within', or 'inside'. It places something inside a state, place, or condition. Here it conveys being immersed in or surrounded by a condition (struggle/hardship).
3.grammar: This is an indeclinable preposition (it never changes form). It governs the noun after it, putting that noun in the genitive case. It has no tense or ending of its own to explain; its whole job is to link 'created humankind' to the state 'in hardship'.

4.meaning: 'On a day' — the preposition 'fī' (in/on) joined to 'a day', setting the occasion of the feeding: feeding done 'on a day' of severe hardship, a time when food is scarce and hunger is widespread.
4.grammar: A preposition 'fī' followed by an indefinite masculine singular noun. The '-in' ending on 'yawm' is genitive with nunation: it is genitive because it is the object of the preposition 'fī' ('on a day') — NOT because of any possessive (iḍāfa) link — and the '-n' marks it as indefinite ('a day'). 'Yawm' is then itself described by what follows ('a day OF hunger').
4.root: ي-و-م (y-w-m) — day, a period of time

5.meaning: 'Possessor of / having' — a word meaning 'owner of' or 'endowed with'. It attributes a quality to what precedes: a day 'possessed of', i.e. characterized by, severe hunger.
5.grammar: A noun of the special 'five nouns' class meaning 'owner of', which must be followed by what is possessed. It is in the genitive case, shown here by the long '-ī' ending (these nouns take 'ī' for genitive instead of a short '-i'). It is genitive because it describes the preceding genitive noun 'day' ('a day HAVING…'), and it links onward to 'hunger'.
5.root: — (a relational noun meaning 'possessor of'; no verbal triliteral root)

6.meaning: Severe hunger, ravenous starvation — intense, gnawing famine. It names the harsh condition that defines the day on which feeding the poor is so meritorious.
6.grammar: An indefinite feminine singular noun (a noun naming a state, on the 'mafʿala' pattern). The '-in' ending is genitive with nunation: genitive because it is the thing possessed by 'dhī' ('having OF hunger'), and the '-n' marks it as indefinite. Together with 'dhī' it describes the day as one 'of severe hunger'.
6.root: س-غ-ب (s-gh-b) — hunger, to be hungry, famine

1.meaning: An orphan — specifically a child whose father has died before the child reaches maturity. The indefinite, accusative form here points to 'a certain orphan' as the object of feeding/giving.

parts.en: indefinite accusative ending ('a/an … ', as direct object)

1.grammar: A singular indefinite noun. The final -an (tanwīn, the doubled 'an' sound written with two strokes) does two jobs at once: the 'n' means 'a/an' (indefinite), and the 'a' vowel is the accusative case, marking it as the object of the verb (the one being fed). The doubled yāʾ at the start (yya-) is simply the running-on of the preceding word in recitation.

2.meaning: 'Possessor of / endowed with / one having' — a connector word meaning the following noun belongs to or characterizes the person. Here 'dhā maqrabah' = 'one possessing kinship', i.e. a relative.
2.grammar: This is one of the 'Five Nouns' that show case with a long vowel instead of a short one. The long -ā ending is the accusative form (it would be dhū in the nominative, dhī in the genitive). The accusative -ā here agrees with the orphan it describes — 'an orphan WHO IS one possessing kinship'. It is always followed by another noun that it 'possesses'.
2.root: — (a connector noun meaning 'possessor of'; no verbal root)

3.meaning: Nearness, closeness — here in the sense of close kinship or family relationship. Paired with the preceding word: 'possessor of kinship', i.e. a near relative.
3.grammar: A noun of place / abstract noun on the mafʿalah pattern (مَفْعَلَة). The final -in (tanwīn kasrah) again carries two meanings: the 'n' means 'a/an' (indefinite), and the 'i' vowel is the genitive case, required because it is 'possessed' by the preceding word dhā — literally 'possessor OF a nearness'. The written -ah (tāʾ marbūṭah) sounds as -at- when this ending is added.
3.root: ق-ر-ب (q-r-b) — being near, close, drawing near

1.meaning: 'Or' — a particle offering an alternative, here presenting a second equally praiseworthy deed beside freeing a slave: emancipation OR feeding the hungry.
1.grammar: An indeclinable conjunction with no case ending. It links two alternatives, joining the act of 'feeding' that follows to the act of 'freeing' that came before, presenting them as parallel options.

2.meaning: A needy, poor person — someone in such want that they are bowed low by it; one lacking the means to meet their basic needs. Indefinite accusative as the object of giving/feeding.

parts.en: indefinite accusative ending ('a … ', as direct object)

2.grammar: A singular indefinite noun on the mifʿīl pattern (often denoting one marked by a state). The final -an (tanwīn fatḥah): the 'n' means 'a/an', and the 'a' vowel is the accusative case, marking it as the object being fed.
2.root: س-ك-ن (s-k-n) — being still, motionless (the poor are 'stilled', held down, by their poverty)

3.meaning: 'Possessor of / endowed with / one having' — a connector word meaning the following noun belongs to or characterizes the person. Here 'dhā maqrabah' = 'one possessing kinship', i.e. a relative.
3.grammar: This is one of the 'Five Nouns' that show case with a long vowel instead of a short one. The long -ā ending is the accusative form (it would be dhū in the nominative, dhī in the genitive). The accusative -ā here agrees with the orphan it describes — 'an orphan WHO IS one possessing kinship'. It is always followed by another noun that it 'possesses'.
3.root: — (a connector noun meaning 'possessor of'; no verbal root)

4.meaning: Destitution, abject misery — literally 'cleaving to the dust', the condition of one so poor they are laid low in the dirt. Describes the depth of the poor person's distress.
4.grammar: An abstract noun on the mafʿalah pattern. The final -in (tanwīn kasrah): the 'n' means 'a/an', and the 'i' vowel is the genitive case, because it is governed by the preceding word dhā ('possessor of'), which is stated explicitly in the verse — miskīnan dhā matrabah, 'a needy person possessed OF destitution'. The written -ah (tāʾ marbūṭah) sounds as -at- before this ending.
4.root: ت-ر-ب (t-r-b) — dust, earth (to be reduced to the dust through poverty)

1.meaning: 'Then / moreover / and above all' — a sequencing particle. It can mark order in time, but here it signals rising importance: 'and then, beyond all the deeds just mentioned, to be of those who believe…'.
1.grammar: An indeclinable connecting particle (it never changes its ending). It joins what follows to what came before, indicating sequence or a step up to something more significant. It carries no case.

2.meaning: 'He was / he came to be / he is' — the verb of being. Often it links a subject to a description; with 'min' here it means 'he became / was one OF…'. In Qur'anic usage it can also express a settled, enduring state rather than mere past time.

parts.en: was / came to be (verb of being)

2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular: 'he was/became'. The final -a is the standard past-tense ending for 'he'. The long -ā- in the middle is a hollow root whose middle letter (wāw) appears as a long vowel here. As an incomplete verb, it normally needs a following predicate to complete the sense ('he was [something]').
2.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — being, existing, coming to be

3.meaning: 'Of / from / among' — a preposition marking origin, source, or partition. Here 'mina alladhīna' = 'one OF / from among those who…', placing the person within a group.
3.grammar: A preposition. Its base form is 'min' (with a silent final n). When the next word begins with the article al-, the n takes a short -a (min → mina) purely to ease pronunciation across the two words; this is a phonological liaison, not a separate piece of meaning. Whatever follows it stands in the genitive case.

4.meaning: 'Those who' — the masculine plural relative pronoun, pointing to a defined group and introducing a description of them: 'those who believed and urged one another…'.
4.grammar: A masculine plural relative pronoun ('those who'). It is indeclinable — its ending never changes for case. The base is alladhī ('the one who'), and the suffix -na marks it as masculine plural and human. It must be completed by a following clause that describes the group (here 'believed…').

5.meaning: 'They believed / came to faith' — they put their trust and security in Allah, affirming and committing to the faith. The form often carries the sense of a faith that began and now stands firm.
5.grammar: A past-tense verb of Form IV, 3rd-person masculine plural: 'they believed'. The suffix -ū means 'they' (masculine plural). The silent alif written after it (the 'otiose alif') is only a spelling convention and is not pronounced. The opening long ā- is part of the Form IV pattern that here gives the sense of entering into faith.
5.root: ء-م-ن (ʾ-m-n) — safety, security, trust (to have faith is to find security in Allah)

6.meaning: 'And they enjoined one another / counselled each other' — they mutually urged and advised one another. The verb form specifically conveys a two-way, reciprocal action among the group.
6.grammar: Prefix wa- = 'and'. The verb is Form VI (the ta-…-ā- pattern), which signals reciprocal, mutual action — 'they advised one another'. It is past tense, 3rd-person masculine plural; because the root's last letter is weak, the 'they' ending appears as -aw (a 'w'-glide) rather than the usual -ū. The trailing silent alif is again only spelling.
6.root: و-ص-ي (w-ṣ-y) — to enjoin, charge, counsel, give a directive

7.meaning: 'To/with patience' — steadfast endurance: the disciplined restraint and perseverance that holds firm under hardship, obligation, and temptation. This is what they urge on one another.
7.grammar: Preposition bi- ('with/to') + the article al- ('the') + the noun. The final -i is the genitive case, which is obligatory after the preposition bi-. Note the article's 'l' is not pronounced separately but doubles the following ṣ (a 'sun letter'), so it reads biṣ-ṣabr. With the verb tawāṣaw, the bi- conveys the thing they urge upon each other.

8.meaning: 'And they enjoined one another / counselled each other' — they mutually urged and advised one another. The verb form specifically conveys a two-way, reciprocal action among the group.
8.grammar: Prefix wa- = 'and'. The verb is Form VI (the ta-…-ā- pattern), which signals reciprocal, mutual action — 'they advised one another'. It is past tense, 3rd-person masculine plural; because the root's last letter is weak, the 'they' ending appears as -aw (a 'w'-glide) rather than the usual -ū. The trailing silent alif is again only spelling.
8.root: و-ص-ي (w-ṣ-y) — to enjoin, charge, counsel, give a directive

9.meaning: The phrase means 'to compassion' or 'to mutual mercy' — the deep, tender mercy that people urge upon one another. In context it completes the idea of believers encouraging each other toward heartfelt compassion. The 'bi-' here carries the sense of mutually enjoining or urging 'with/to' compassion.
9.grammar: A noun of compassion ('marḥama') with the definite article 'al-' and the preposition 'bi-' attached in front. The final '-i' (kasra) is the genitive case ending, required because any noun after the preposition 'bi-' must take this ending — so 'bi-l-marḥamat-i' = 'with/to the compassion.' The original closing 'h' of marḥamah appears here as 't' (marḥamat-) because it is now followed by a case vowel and joined to the sentence.

1.meaning: A demonstrative pronoun meaning 'those (people)' or 'these' — pointing emphatically to a group just mentioned, as in 'Those are the ones...' It singles them out for the description that follows.
1.grammar: A fixed plural demonstrative pronoun, 'those people.' It does not change for case — its form stays the same whether it is subject or object. The '-ka' element points the listener toward the group ('those over there'). Here it functions as the subject: 'Those are the companions of the right.'

2.meaning: Means 'companions of,' 'people of,' or 'those who belong to / are associated with' something. It denotes the inhabitants or rightful members of a group or place — here, the people who belong to 'the right hand.'
2.grammar: The broken (irregular) plural of 'ṣāḥib' (companion), meaning 'companions/people of.' The final '-u' (ḍamma) is the nominative case ending, marking it as the predicate of the sentence ('Those ARE the companions...'). It is in a possessive construction with the next word, so it means 'companions OF...'

3.meaning: Means 'the right side' or 'the right hand,' and by extension 'the side of good fortune and blessedness.' In Qur'anic imagery the right hand symbolizes those favored and saved — 'the people of the right' are the blessed.

parts.en: right side / right hand / good fortune

3.grammar: A noun meaning 'the right hand / right side / blessedness,' with the definite article 'al-.' The final '-i' (kasra) is the genitive case ending, because it is the second term of a possessive phrase: 'companions OF the right hand' (aṣḥābu l-maymanat-i). The closing 'h' of maymanah surfaces as 't' here because a case vowel follows it.
3.root: ي-م-ن (y-m-n) — the right side; also good fortune, blessing, auspiciousness

1.meaning: Means 'and those who...' — a connector 'and/but' joined to the relative pronoun 'those who,' introducing a group that will be defined by the action described next (here, those who disbelieved).
1.grammar: The connecting particle 'wa-' ('and/but') attached to the masculine plural relative pronoun 'alladhīna' ('those who'). This relative pronoun has a fixed form and does not change for case; here it serves as the subject, awaiting its description: 'and those who disbelieved...' It contrasts this group with the people of the right just mentioned.
1.root: — (connective particle + relative pronoun; no triliteral root)

2.meaning: Means 'they disbelieved' or 'they rejected faith' — they actively denied and covered over the truth. The root sense is 'to cover/conceal,' so disbelief is pictured as covering up a truth one has recognized.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 'to disbelieve/reject.' The ending '-ū' (with the silent 'alif' written after it) is the subject marker meaning 'they' (masculine plural). So 'kafar-ū' = 'they disbelieved.' The action is completed (past tense). It is the verb that defines the relative pronoun before it: 'those who disbelieved.'
2.root: ك-ف-ر (k-f-r) — to cover/conceal; hence to deny, reject, be ungrateful, disbelieve

3.meaning: Means 'in/with Our signs' or 'Our verses.' The word 'āyāt' denotes signs, tokens, or miraculous proofs — and the revealed verses of the Qur'an are called this. 'Our' refers to Allah. The full sense: they disbelieved 'in Our signs/verses.'
3.grammar: The preposition 'bi-' ('in/with') + 'āyāt' ('signs/verses,' the feminine plural of 'āyah') + the attached pronoun '-nā' ('our'). The verb 'to disbelieve' is completed by 'bi-' ('to disbelieve IN'). The case vowel '-i' (genitive) is required after 'bi-' and sits before the possessive 'our.' So: 'in Our signs/verses.'
3.root: ا-ي-ي / ء-ي-ي (ʾ-y-y) — sign, mark, token (root of 'āyah')

4.meaning: An independent pronoun meaning 'they' (masculine plural). Standing on its own it adds emphasis — 'they (and they specifically)' — and here begins a new statement: 'they are the people of the left.'
4.grammar: A standalone subject pronoun, 'they' (masculine plural). It is fixed in form and does not take case endings. Placed at the start of a clause it acts as the subject and gives emphasis: 'They — they are the companions of the left.' It restates and stresses the group already introduced.

5.meaning: Means 'companions of,' 'people of,' or 'those who belong to / are associated with' something. It denotes the inhabitants or rightful members of a group or place — here, the people who belong to 'the right hand.'
5.grammar: The broken (irregular) plural of 'ṣāḥib' (companion), meaning 'companions/people of.' The final '-u' (ḍamma) is the nominative case ending, marking it as the predicate of the sentence ('Those ARE the companions...'). It is in a possessive construction with the next word, so it means 'companions OF...'

6.meaning: Means 'the left side' or 'the left hand,' and by extension 'the side of ill fortune, misery, and condemnation.' In Qur'anic imagery the left hand marks those who are doomed — 'the people of the left' are the wretched.

parts.en: left side / left hand / ill fortune

6.grammar: A noun meaning 'the left hand / left side / ill-omen,' with the definite article 'al-.' Note the hamza (ʾ) in the middle: it is a root consonant (ش-ء-م), so the word is transliterated 'mashʾama,' not 'mashama.' The final '-i' (kasra) is the genitive case ending, because it is the second term of a possessive phrase: '(the) companions OF the left hand' (aṣḥābu l-mashʾamat-i). The closing 'h' of mashʾamah surfaces as 't' because a case vowel follows it.
6.root: ش-ء-م (sh-ʾ-m) — the left side; also ill fortune, bad omen, wretchedness

1.meaning: Means 'over them' or 'upon them' — the preposition 'over/upon' joined to the pronoun 'them' (masculine plural). It conveys something pressing down on or enclosing them from above: 'over them (will be a Fire).'
1.grammar: The preposition 'ʿalā' ('over/upon'), which shifts to the form 'ʿalay-' when a pronoun is attached, plus '-him' ('them,' masculine plural). The pronoun takes the form '-him' (rather than '-hum') because it follows the 'i'-vowel of 'ʿalay.' Together: 'over them.' The phrase is fronted for emphasis: 'over them (is) a Fire.'

2.meaning: Means 'a fire' — and here specifically the Fire of punishment (Hell). Presented indefinitely ('a Fire'), it conveys awe and severity: an overwhelming fire enclosing the condemned.
2.grammar: A feminine noun, 'fire.' The ending '-un' (ḍamma with 'tanwīn,' the doubled vowel sound) marks two things at once: the nominative case (it is the subject — 'a Fire' is what will be over them) and indefiniteness ('a fire,' not 'the fire'). So 'nār-un' = 'a fire.'

3.meaning: Means 'closed in / shut over / sealed tight.' It describes the Fire as completely enclosing its inhabitants — a vault locked shut upon them with no way out, sealing in the heat and the punishment.

parts.en: prefix forming a passive descriptor ('being made...')
shut / closed over / sealed (passive participle stem)

3.grammar: A passive participle, 'closed in / shut over,' built on the Form IV pattern 'mufʿalah' (the 'mu-' prefix makes it a passive descriptor — 'one that is shut'). The feminine marker is the tā marbūṭa ('-t-'), which agrees with 'nār' (fire, feminine); it is a separate morpheme from the case ending. The final '-un' (ḍamma + 'tanwīn') is the nominative, indefinite ending, because it describes the indefinite subject 'a fire': 'a Fire, shut tight over them' (nār-un muʾṣadat-un). The doubled 'm' at the start results from the previous word's '-n' merging (idghām) into it.
3.root: و-ص-د / ء-ص-د (w-ṣ-d / ʾ-ṣ-d) — to close, shut, fasten over
